| LANG-C01 | 01_lang | js-principle | consensus | Module code and class bodies are always strict mode code, so they need no use strict directive. | - |
| LANG-C02 | 01_lang | practice | single-source | Run all code in strict mode: write ES modules or classes (strict by construction) and add the use strict directive only to classic scripts, because strict mode turns silent errors into thrown errors. | folklore: strict mode is just a stricter subset of the language |
| LANG-C03 | 01_lang | js-principle | single-source | In strict mode, assigning to an undeclared identifier throws a ReferenceError; in sloppy mode it silently creates a global property, so a typo becomes a global variable. | - |
| LANG-C04 | 01_lang | js-principle | consensus | Never rely on an implicit global this: in a plain function call this is undefined in strict code and globalThis in sloppy code. | - |
| LANG-C05 | 01_lang | js-principle | consensus | A function's this is set by how it is called, not where it is defined: a method detached from its object (callback, variable) loses its receiver and sees undefined in strict code. | - |

| LANG-C09 | 01_lang | js-principle | single-source | Do not use a class before its declaration is evaluated: class declarations sit in the temporal dead zone like let and const and are not hoisted. | - |
| LANG-C10 | 01_lang | js-principle | consensus | In a derived class call super() before touching this; the derived class's field initialisers run right after super() returns, the base class's at the start of its constructor. | - |
| LANG-C11 | 01_lang | practice | consensus | Use # private fields when real encapsulation is needed: access from outside the class is a SyntaxError and there is no reflective backdoor. | - |

| ASYNC-C01 | 03_async | practice | consensus | Always return (or await) a promise created inside a then callback; a promise that is started but not returned is lost to the chain and later handlers run early on incomplete data. | folklore: a missing return in a then callback is harmless |
| ASYNC-C02 | 03_async | practice | consensus | Never leave a promise floating: every created promise must be awaited, returned, or given a rejection handler (catch, or then with two arguments), because an unhandled rejection is a runtime error event. | - |
| ASYNC-C03 | 03_async | practice | single-source | Do not treat the void operator as handling a promise: it only silences the lint rule and changes no runtime behaviour. | - |
| ASYNC-C04 | 03_async | js-principle | consensus | In Node an unhandled promise rejection is raised as an uncaught exception, so a rejected promise nobody handles can terminate the process; this has been the default since Node 15. | folklore: unhandled rejections only print a warning; boundary: 09_runtime (process lifecycle) |
| ASYNC-C05 | 03_async | practice | single-source | Treat the unhandledRejection and uncaughtException hooks as last-resort reporting points, never as a way to carry on: after an uncaught exception the application state is undefined and resuming is unsafe. | boundary: 09_runtime |
| ASYNC-C06 | 03_async | js-principle | consensus | In a browser, handle unhandled rejections through the cancelable unhandledrejection event on the global scope (window or worker); preventDefault suppresses the console report, and cross-origin script rejections do not fire it. | - |
| ASYNC-C07 | 03_async | js-principle | consensus | An async function always returns a new promise and converts every uncaught exception inside it into a rejection; callers must therefore handle the rejection, not catch synchronously. | - |
| ASYNC-C08 | 03_async | practice | single-source | Never await two already-started promises one after the other when the second can reject before the first settles; combine them with Promise.all or Promise.allSettled first. | - |
| ASYNC-C09 | 03_async | js-principle | consensus | Know that Promise.all rejects as soon as one input rejects but the other operations keep running with their outcomes unavailable; use Promise.allSettled when every operation must finish before continuing. | folklore: Promise.all or race cancels the losing operations |
| ASYNC-C10 | 03_async | practice | consensus | Run independent asynchronous operations concurrently (Promise.all over the started promises), not in a sequential loop of awaits, unless a later operation depends on an earlier result. | positions: MDN: run concurrently unless dependent |
| ASYNC-C11 | 03_async | practice | single-source | Do not pass an async function as the executor of new Promise: an error thrown in it is lost and does not reject the new promise; usually the constructor is unnecessary. | - |
| ASYNC-C12 | 03_async | practice | consensus | Do not wrap an existing promise in new Promise (the explicit-constructor pattern); return the promise itself, which keeps rejections flowing; use util.promisify rather than hand-written promisification of error-first callbacks. | - |
| ASYNC-C13 | 03_async | practice | single-source | Ensure every promise you construct settles on every code path and is resolved or rejected exactly once; a promise that never settles silently kills all its reactions, and a second resolve has no effect. | - |
| ASYNC-C14 | 03_async | practice | single-source | Return the promise produced by p.then(...), not the original p, when chaining; returning p forks the chain and the continuation result is lost. | - |
| ASYNC-C15 | 03_async | practice | single-source | MDN's editorial position: keep promise chains flat, and nest only deliberately to limit the scope of a catch (an inner catch handles only failures in its own scope). | positions: MDN: flat chains by default |
| ASYNC-C16 | 03_async | practice | consensus | Do not pass an async function where a void-returning callback is expected (event handlers, array callbacks such as forEach): the returned promise is dropped and its rejection goes unhandled; catch inside the handler instead. | - |
| ASYNC-C17 | 03_async | practice | single-source | Never use a promise as a condition (if, ternary, logical operators): a Promise object is always truthy; await it first. | - |
| ASYNC-C18 | 03_async | practice | consensus | Throw and reject only with Error instances (or subclasses), never strings or plain objects, because Error objects record where they were created. | positions: typescript-eslint: throw Error only; Google JS guide: always throw Error or subclasses |
| ASYNC-C19 | 03_async | practice | consensus | When catching and rethrowing, wrap with a more specific message and pass the original as the cause option so the original error stays available; do not assume the cause is an Error. | - |
| ASYNC-C20 | 03_async | practice | single-source | Use cause for one failing site only; to represent several failures at once use AggregateError (or SuppressedError). | - |
| ASYNC-C21 | 03_async | practice | single-source | The Google JavaScript Style Guide's position: an empty catch block is very rarely correct, and when no action is right the reason is explained in a comment. | positions: Google JS guide: justify empty catch in a comment |
| ASYNC-C22 | 03_async | js-principle | single-source | In Node, a throw inside an asynchronous callback cannot be intercepted by a surrounding try/catch; report errors through the promise rejection, the error-first callback argument, or an emitter error event. | - |
| ASYNC-C23 | 03_async | practice | consensus | Always attach an error listener to every EventEmitter (sockets, streams, servers): an emitted error event without a listener is thrown and can crash the process, which is also a denial-of-service vector. | boundary: 06_runsec (DoS) |
| ASYNC-C24 | 03_async | practice | single-source | Identify Node errors by error.code, not error.message, because messages may change between versions. | - |
| ASYNC-C25 | 03_async | js-principle | consensus | Do not assume promises are cancellable: Promise has no cancellation protocol; cancel the underlying operation, typically with AbortController. | folklore: promises can be cancelled |
| ASYNC-C26 | 03_async | practice | consensus | Design cancellable async APIs to accept an AbortSignal option and, on abort, reject any unsettled promise with the signal's reason. | - |
| ASYNC-C27 | 03_async | practice | consensus | Start such an API by calling signal.throwIfAborted() so an already-aborted signal rejects immediately. | - |
| ASYNC-C28 | 03_async | practice | consensus | Put timeouts on awaited operations with AbortSignal.timeout(ms), which rejects with a TimeoutError distinct from a user AbortError; combine a user signal and a timeout with AbortSignal.any, accepting that the combined signal cannot say which fired first by name. | note: MDN says any() cannot tell a timeout from an abort; Node documents that the combined reason is the causing signal's reason, so the two are compatible, not contested |
| ASYNC-C29 | 03_async | js-principle | consensus | An AbortSignal is one-shot: once aborted it stays aborted, the abort event fires once, and later uses of the same signal reject immediately; create a new controller per operation. | - |
| ASYNC-C30 | 03_async | practice | single-source | Remove abort listeners when the operation ends (once option or removeEventListener in finally), because signals from AbortSignal.any and AbortSignal.timeout stay alive while they have sources, pending timeouts and listeners. | - |
| ASYNC-C31 | 03_async | js-principle | consensus | Do not rely on timer precision: a timer delay is a lower bound, the callback may run later and in unspecified relative order; sleeping with a timer never guarantees an exact time. | folklore: setTimeout(fn, 0) runs at once or exactly on time |
| ASYNC-C32 | 03_async | js-principle | consensus | Know the delay clamps: browsers clamp nested timers (nesting level above 5) to at least 4 ms; Node sets delays below 1, NaN or above 2147483647 to 1 ms. | folklore: 0 ms timers fire with no delay |
| ASYNC-C33 | 03_async | js-principle | single-source | Pass a function, not a string, to setTimeout and setInterval: a string handler is compiled as a classic script, equivalent to eval, and is subject to CSP and Trusted Types checks. | boundary: 05_domsec |
| ASYNC-C34 | 03_async | practice | single-source | In Node prefer the timers/promises variants with a signal option for cancellable waiting, and clear or unref timers that must not keep the process alive. | boundary: 09_runtime (process lifecycle) |
| ASYNC-C35 | 03_async | js-principle | consensus | Promise reactions never run synchronously, even for an already settled promise: they run as microtasks after the current run completes and the stack is empty, before the event loop returns to timers and I/O. | folklore: then on a resolved promise runs immediately |
| ASYNC-C36 | 03_async | practice | single-source | Prefer setImmediate over process.nextTick for deferring work, because a recursive nextTick loop starves I/O and never lets the loop reach the poll phase. | folklore: nextTick is the right general-purpose way to defer |
| ASYNC-C37 | 03_async | js-principle | consensus | Do not depend on the order of setTimeout(0) versus setImmediate outside an I/O callback (non-deterministic); inside an I/O callback the immediate always runs first. | - |
| ASYNC-C38 | 03_async | principle | consensus | Do not block the event loop: Node serves every client from few threads, so a callback that runs long delays all clients (throughput loss) and gives an attacker a denial-of-service lever. | boundary: 09_runtime (performance) |
| ASYNC-C39 | 03_async | practice | single-source | Keep per-callback cost bounded relative to input size: reason about the computational complexity of each callback and the possible length of its arguments, including JSON.parse and JSON.stringify, which are linear but can take surprisingly long on large input. | - |
| ASYNC-C40 | 03_async | js-principle | consensus | A regular expression match runs uninterrupted on the main thread and cannot be split into chunks, so one request with a pathological input can block a Node server for seconds; in a 2018 study 25 new vulnerabilities were found in popular modules and 339 of 2,846 tested popular sites were affected. | boundary: 06_runsec (ReDoS rules) |
| ASYNC-C41 | 03_async | practice | single-source | Treat synchronous core APIs (sync crypto, compression, file system, child process) as event-loop blockers in a server; the mechanism is that they run on the event loop thread. | - |
| ASYNC-C42 | 03_async | practice | single-source | Partition long computations on the event loop into small steps that yield between them (for instance with setImmediate) so other pending events get turns. | - |
| ASYNC-C43 | 03_async | decision | consensus | Use workers for CPU-intensive JavaScript, not for I/O: built-in asynchronous I/O is more efficient than workers can be. | - |
| ASYNC-C44 | 03_async | practice | single-source | Use workers sparingly: the HTML Standard calls them relatively heavy-weight with high startup cost and per-instance memory, not intended to be used in large numbers. | - |
| ASYNC-C45 | 03_async | js-principle | consensus | Message data between threads is copied by structured clone; transfer large buffers via the transfer list (the sender loses them) or share memory with SharedArrayBuffer, and expect no DOM access inside browser workers. | - |
| ASYNC-C46 | 03_async | practice | consensus | Handle both the error and exit events of a Worker (and onerror and messageerror in browsers): an uncaught exception in the worker terminates it and surfaces only as events. | - |
| ASYNC-C47 | 03_async | practice | single-source | Cap worker resources with resourceLimits where untrusted input drives the work; reaching a limit terminates the worker. | boundary: 09_runtime |
| ASYNC-C48 | 03_async | practice | single-source | Use AsyncLocalStorage, not a hand-built async_hooks layer, to carry request-scoped state across callbacks and promise chains; prefer run() over enterWith(), which leaks the context into later handlers. | - |
| ASYNC-C49 | 03_async | decision | single-source | Do not rely on AsyncContext in the language: it is a TC39 proposal at stage 2, so portable code uses AsyncLocalStorage in Node only. | - |
| ASYNC-C50 | 03_async | decision | single-source | The WICG Prioritized Task Scheduling API (scheduler.postTask, scheduler.yield, TaskController with abort and priority) is a draft for engines that ship it; Node exposes only experimental timers/promises scheduler.wait and scheduler.yield. | - |
| ASYNC-C51 | 03_async | practice | single-source | The stage-4 promise and error features have these edition years: Promise.allSettled 2020, Promise.any 2021, Error cause 2022, top-level await 2022, Promise.withResolvers 2024, Promise.try 2025, Array.fromAsync 2026. | - |
| ASYNC-C52 | 03_async | decision | single-source | In 2018 the V8 team advised favouring async functions and await over hand-written promise code, after reducing await to one microtask tick for native promises (V8 7.2); the old claim that await costs three ticks is obsolete. | folklore: async/await is slower than promise chains |
| ASYNC-C53 | 03_async | practice | single-source | Avoid creating promises that do no work: an async function with no await, an await on the returned value, and Promise.resolve().then(f) each add promises that DrAsync flags and that can usually be refactored. | - |
| ASYNC-C54 | 03_async | practice | single-source | Guard read-modify-write of shared variables across an await or yield: the value may have changed while the function was suspended. | - |
| ASYNC-C55 | 03_async | practice | single-source | Configure HTTP server timeouts (headersTimeout, requestTimeout, timeout, keepAliveTimeout) so slow or idle connections are dropped; slow requests otherwise hold resources. | boundary: 06_runsec |
| STRUCT-C01 | 04_struct | js-principle | consensus | Do not write to an imported binding; ask the exporting module to change it, because an import is a read-only live view that only the exporter can reassign. | - |
| STRUCT-C02 | 04_struct | js-principle | consensus | Treat an exported object as shared mutable state: importers cannot rebind it but can still modify its properties, so freeze it or hide it behind functions if mutation is not intended. | boundary: 01 LANG (freeze mechanics) |
| STRUCT-C03 | 04_struct | practice | single-source | Guide Google JS holds that exported variables must not be mutated outside module initialization; guide Google TS bans `export let`; guide Airbnb holds that mutable bindings are not exported. | - |
| STRUCT-C04 | 04_struct | js-principle | consensus | Do not rely on import statement order to sequence work: import declarations are hoisted and the imported module's side effects run before the rest of the importing module's code. | - |
| STRUCT-C05 | 04_struct | js-principle | consensus | Treat top-level code of a module as running once, at first import, for every importer; to run code repeatedly, export a function and call it. | - |
| STRUCT-C06 | 04_struct | practice | single-source | Keep module top level free of side effects other than initialising its own exports, so that importing it is safe in any order and unused code can be dropped by tools. | - |
| STRUCT-C07 | 04_struct | practice | consensus | Use a bare `import "x"` only for the module's side effect (polyfills, global registration), and name it as such. | - |
| STRUCT-C08 | 04_struct | js-principle | consensus | Expect a cycle between modules to fail only when a binding is used while uninitialised, not at load time; in CommonJS the cyclic importer receives an unfinished copy of the exports object. | folklore: cyclic imports always crash |
| STRUCT-C09 | 04_struct | decision | contested | Cycles between modules: whether to forbid them is contested (MDN usually avoid; Google JS no cycles; eslint-plugin-import always a dangerous anti-pattern; Node documents cycles as a supported loading mechanism). | positions: MDN: usually avoid, error-prone; Google JS: do not create cycles even though the spec allows them; eslint-plugin-import maintainers: always a dangerous anti-pattern, no evidence given; Node CJS docs: cycles are supported via partial exports, no recommendation. Applies to ESM and CJS alike, none states a measured cost |
| STRUCT-C10 | 04_struct | practice | single-source | A lint rule can detect cycles but is comparatively expensive; enable it knowingly (eslint-plugin-import no-cycle, with maxDepth to bound cost). | - |
| STRUCT-C11 | 04_struct | practice | consensus | In Node ESM, write the file extension on relative specifiers and spell out directory indexes, as in browsers. | - |
| STRUCT-C12 | 04_struct | practice | single-source | Guide Google JS holds that the .js extension is never optional in import paths. | - |
| STRUCT-C13 | 04_struct | practice | consensus | In Node ESM, replace CommonJS globals: use import.meta.dirname and import.meta.filename (or new URL with import.meta.url) instead of __dirname and __filename, module.createRequire where require is needed, and a with { type: "json" } attribute for JSON. | - |
| STRUCT-C14 | 04_struct | practice | single-source | Declare module format explicitly (.mjs or .cjs extension, or the package.json "type" field) and do not rely on syntax detection for .js files. | - |
| STRUCT-C15 | 04_struct | js-principle | consensus | When importing CommonJS from ESM, do not depend on named imports for unusual export patterns: Node finds named exports by static analysis of common syntax and it does not always detect them; the default import is always the module.exports object. | - |
| STRUCT-C16 | 04_struct | js-principle | consensus | require() of an ES module works only if the module graph has no top-level await; otherwise Node throws ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE. require(esm) is no longer experimental as of Node 25.4.0. | folklore: CommonJS cannot load ESM |
| STRUCT-C17 | 04_struct | practice | consensus | Never assign to the CommonJS exports variable to replace the export: it detaches from module.exports and the assignment is not exported; assign module.exports instead. | - |
| STRUCT-C18 | 04_struct | js-principle | consensus | Treat a module that uses top-level await as an asynchronous dependency: every importer's body waits for it, siblings are not blocked, and a never-resolving await makes Node exit with status 13. | - |
| STRUCT-C19 | 04_struct | decision | contested | Whether top-level await is a footgun is disputed inside the proposal record: critics fear coordination and deadlock surprises; the champions answer with education and note deadlocks already exist. | positions: critics recorded in the proposal: top-level await is a footgun; champions Borins and Startsev: education suffices, deadlock risk already exists, import() inside TLA costs the same. Applies to any module graph; no measurement given |
| STRUCT-C20 | 04_struct | practice | consensus | Use dynamic import() for conditional or deferred loading; static import declarations are top-level only, hoisted and unconditional. | - |
| STRUCT-C21 | 04_struct | js-principle | consensus | Modules are strict mode and deferred by default; do not add defer to module scripts and do not expect classic-script behaviour. | boundary: 01 LANG |
| STRUCT-C22 | 04_struct | js-principle | consensus | Do not rely on `export * from` to merge modules whose export names may collide: a name exported by two wildcard re-exports is silently omitted from the result. | - |
| STRUCT-C23 | 04_struct | js-principle | consensus | Duplicate export names and more than one default export are a SyntaxError that prevents the module from being evaluated. | - |
| STRUCT-C24 | 04_struct | decision | contested | Named versus default exports is contested: Google JS and Google TS ban default exports; Airbnb prefers a default export in single-export modules; MDN presents default exports as designed for easy default functions and CommonJS and AMD interoperation. | positions: Google JS and Google TS: named only, because a default export has no canonical name and encourages one namespacing object; Airbnb: prefer default when a module has a single export; MDN: neutral, names the interop purpose. Applies to application and library modules alike; the tooling reason (rename refactors) is the guides' own |
| STRUCT-C25 | 04_struct | practice | single-source | Guide Google TS holds that only symbols used outside a module are exported and the exported API surface is minimised. | boundary: 02 TYPES |
| STRUCT-C26 | 04_struct | practice | single-source | Guides Google JS and Google TS hold that classes with only static members are not used as a namespace; export individual functions and constants from the module instead. | - |
| STRUCT-C27 | 04_struct | practice | single-source | Guide Google TS holds that namespaces are banned and code refers to other files only through ES module imports and exports. | boundary: 02 TYPES |
| STRUCT-C28 | 04_struct | practice | single-source | Guide Google TS holds that relative imports are used for files of the same logical project, so a project can move without rewriting imports. | boundary: 02 TYPES |
| STRUCT-C29 | 04_struct | decision | single-source | A barrel file (a module that only re-exports) makes every importer load all re-exported modules eagerly; one author measured empty-module loading at 0.15 s for 500 modules and 48.44 s for 50,000 on one laptop and holds that barrel files should go. | positions: Hagemeister: remove barrels (synthetic, one machine, T3); MDN: barrel modules are a documented use of aggregation, no recommendation |
| STRUCT-C30 | 04_struct | js-principle | consensus | Tree shaking relies on the static structure of import and export; a bundler needs hints (webpack: package.json sideEffects, /*#__PURE__*/) where code does something on import beyond exporting. | boundary: 08 QUALITY |
| STRUCT-C31 | 04_struct | js-principle | consensus | Node does not read the sideEffects field: package.json fields of other tools are ignored by Node. | - |
| STRUCT-C32 | 04_struct | decision | single-source | Position of V8 (2018): keep bundling for production (apps over about 100 modules or with dependency depth under 5) while writing small fine-grained modules. | - |
| STRUCT-C33 | 04_struct | practice | consensus | Define the package.json "exports" field to declare a package's public entry points: it encapsulates every other subpath, giving tools and semver handling reliable interface guarantees. | boundary: 07 SUPPLY |
| STRUCT-C34 | 04_struct | js-principle | consensus | Adding "exports" to an existing package is a breaking change for consumers that deep-import, and the encapsulation is not strong: an absolute file path still loads. | boundary: 07 SUPPLY |
| STRUCT-C35 | 04_struct | practice | consensus | In conditional exports, order keys from most specific to least specific and put "default" last, because earlier entries take priority. | - |
| STRUCT-C36 | 04_struct | practice | consensus | Use the package.json "imports" field (keys starting with #) for package-internal aliases: Node resolves them natively and they cannot collide with external package names. | - |
| STRUCT-C37 | 04_struct | js-principle | consensus | Module resolution is defined by the host, not by ECMAScript, so an import specifier can mean different things in Node, a browser and a bundler; configure the type checker to match the host that runs the code. | boundary: 02 TYPES |
| STRUCT-C38 | 04_struct | practice | consensus | When files are transpiled one at a time (Babel, swc, esbuild), enable TypeScript isolatedModules so code that needs cross-file information is reported. | boundary: 02 TYPES |
| STRUCT-C39 | 04_struct | js-principle | consensus | Use `#` private elements when privacy must be enforced: the language enforces them, subclasses and outside code cannot reach them, and they cannot be proxied, enumerated, deleted, cloned by structuredClone, or affected by freeze and seal. | - |
| STRUCT-C40 | 04_struct | js-principle | consensus | A leading underscore does not make a member private; MDN notes that WeakMap and closure emulations of privacy cannot match the # syntax. | folklore: an underscore prefix keeps a member private |
| STRUCT-C41 | 04_struct | decision | contested | How to mark private members is contested: MDN presents # as hard privacy; Google JS allows an optional trailing underscore for private fields; Airbnb bans leading and trailing underscores because they are public API; Google TS bans # and uses TypeScript private for emit-size and performance reasons. | positions: MDN: # for hard privacy; Google JS: optional trailing underscore on private names; Airbnb: no underscores, since they are public API contract; Google TS: TypeScript private not #, because down-levelling # costs emit size and performance. Applies per target: native ES2022 versus down-levelled TypeScript output |
| STRUCT-C42 | 04_struct | practice | consensus | Do not create functions inside functions where no closure is needed: every function instance carries its own scope and closure, costing speed and memory. | boundary: 09 RUNTIME |
| STRUCT-C43 | 04_struct | practice | consensus | Set an object's prototype at creation; changing it later with setPrototypeOf or __proto__ disrupts engine optimisations and may cause deoptimising recompilation. | - |
| STRUCT-C44 | 04_struct | practice | consensus | Do not add methods to built-in prototypes (monkey patching): if the language later adds the same name with a different signature your code breaks, as in SmooshGate; the only good reason MDN names is backporting. | folklore: never subclass built-ins (the warning targets patching built-in prototypes, not subclassing) |
| STRUCT-C45 | 04_struct | js-principle | consensus | Use hasOwn or hasOwnProperty to test own properties: iteration and lookup traverse the prototype chain, and a missing property walks the whole chain. | boundary: 01 LANG |
| STRUCT-C46 | 04_struct | practice | single-source | Guide Google JS holds that getter and setter properties are not used; ordinary methods are provided instead, as getters and setters are potentially surprising and hard to reason about. | - |
| STRUCT-C47 | 04_struct | practice | single-source | ESLint documents the reason to cap positional parameters: numerous parameters are hard to read and write because each parameter, its type and its order must be memorised. | - |
| STRUCT-C48 | 04_struct | practice | single-source | W3C TAG holds that optional and primitive arguments are accepted through a dictionary (options object) and that arguments are made optional where possible. | - |
| STRUCT-C49 | 04_struct | practice | single-source | Prefer an options object over a long positional parameter list when several arguments are optional or of the same primitive type. | - |
| STRUCT-C50 | 04_struct | practice | single-source | TypeScript handbook holds that, in declared APIs, optional trailing parameters replace overloads that differ only in trailing parameters, because overloads let a wrongly typed function pass compatibility and break explicit undefined under strict null checks. | boundary: 02 TYPES |
| STRUCT-C51 | 04_struct | practice | single-source | TypeScript handbook holds that a union type replaces overloads that differ in the type of one argument position, so callers passing a through-value of the union type are accepted. | boundary: 02 TYPES |
| STRUCT-C52 | 04_struct | practice | single-source | TypeScript handbook holds that a callback whose result is ignored is typed void not any, and its parameters are not optional, because it is always legal to supply a callback accepting fewer arguments. | boundary: 02 TYPES |
| STRUCT-C53 | 04_struct | practice | single-source | W3C TAG holds that asynchronous APIs return Promises for one-shot operations and are cancelled with an AbortSignal. | boundary: 03 ASYNC |
| STRUCT-C54 | 04_struct | decision | single-source | W3C TAG holds that a class is shaped for state: classes should have constructors when possible, and stateless groupings are static methods rather than fake classes. | - |
| STRUCT-C55 | 04_struct | practice | single-source | Name identifiers with whole words, not single letters or abbreviations: in an experiment with 72 professional C# developers, words gave about 19 percent faster comprehension in finding defects than letters or abbreviations, with no significant difference between letters and abbreviations. | - |
| STRUCT-C56 | 04_struct | practice | single-source | Guides hold that names are descriptive and not abbreviated by deleting letters (Google JS and Google TS), consistent and made of common words (W3C TAG), and descriptive (Airbnb). | - |
| STRUCT-C57 | 04_struct | practice | single-source | Expect two developers to pick the same name for a thing only rarely (median 6.9 percent over 47 instances), but a chosen name is usually understood; name by selecting concepts, choosing words per concept, then composing the name. | - |
| STRUCT-C58 | 04_struct | principle | single-source | Decompose a system into modules by listing difficult or likely-to-change design decisions and hiding each in one module, not by the steps of processing. | - |
| STRUCT-C59 | 04_struct | principle | single-source | Keep each module's public surface minimal at all three levels: named exports of an ES module, the package "exports" field, and `#` class members. | - |
| STRUCT-C60 | 04_struct | practice | single-source | Dependency direction between layers (which module kinds may import which) should be declared and enforced mechanically, with ESLint no-restricted-imports as one mechanism. | - |
| STRUCT-C61 | 04_struct | practice | consensus | ESLint no-restricted-imports forbids named modules by exact path or by gitignore-style pattern, with custom messages and importNames. | - |
| STRUCT-C62 | 04_struct | principle | single-source | An abstract data type hides a representation behind operations; an object exports a procedural interface and hides information by procedural abstraction; the two differ and should not be conflated when designing a JavaScript API. | - |
| STRUCT-C63 | 04_struct | decision | contested | Whether a paradigm (functional, procedural, object-oriented) lowers defects is contested: Ray et al. report a modest language effect with functional somewhat better than procedural, the reproduction finds only four of eleven languages significant with exceedingly small effects, and the original authors answer that the reproduction largely replicated them. | positions: Ray et al. 2014: modest effect, functional somewhat better than procedural, strong typing modestly better than weak, process factors dominate; Berger et al. 2019 reproduction: flaws, only four languages significant, effect size exceedingly small; Ray, Devanbu, Filkov rebuttal: results largely replicated, effects small, absence of effect possible. Applies to language-level comparison across 17 languages, not to paradigm inside JavaScript |
| STRUCT-C64 | 04_struct | decision | single-source | Choose the paradigm per problem by intent; no admitted source supports choosing an object-oriented or functional style inside JavaScript on defect-rate evidence. | - |
| STRUCT-C65 | 04_struct | principle | single-source | State kept in more than one place can become inconsistent: Codd defines a state as consistent or inconsistent according as its value satisfies declared constraint statements, and treats redundancy and consistency together. | - |
| STRUCT-C66 | 04_struct | principle | single-source | Separate immutability (no one can change state) from read-only restriction (only some clients may); language support for both is long argued by practitioners, but this paper shows no effect evidence. | boundary: 01 LANG |
| STRUCT-C67 | 04_struct | practice | single-source | Do not assume a minor or patch release of an npm dependency is non-breaking: the study found 44 percent of manifesting breaking changes arrived in minor and patch releases. | boundary: 07 SUPPLY |
| DOMSEC-C01 | 05_domsec | practice | consensus | Never assign untrusted data to HTML-parsing sinks (innerHTML, outerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML, document.write, document.writeln); use a safe DOM API or a sanitizer. | - |
| DOMSEC-C02 | 05_domsec | practice | consensus | Insert untrusted text with textContent, or build nodes with createElement and appendChild; never build markup from strings. | - |
| DOMSEC-C03 | 05_domsec | practice | consensus | Never pass untrusted strings to eval, the Function constructors, or the string form of setTimeout and setInterval. | boundary: 06_runsec |
| DOMSEC-C04 | 05_domsec | practice | consensus | Do not place untrusted data inside JavaScript code, event-handler attributes, or script and style contexts at all; encoding is context specific and unreliable there. | - |
| DOMSEC-C05 | 05_domsec | practice | single-source | Quote every inserted attribute value in templates; an unquoted placeholder lets an attacker add an event-handler attribute. | - |
| DOMSEC-C06 | 05_domsec | principle | consensus | Reason about DOM XSS as an attacker-controlled source reaching a dangerous sink, and audit both ends of every flow. | - |
| DOMSEC-C07 | 05_domsec | principle | single-source | Treat sinks beyond XSS as injection points too: location (open redirection), document.cookie, postMessage, web storage setItem, JSON.parse, setAttribute and similar. | positions: restricted T3, catalogue facts only |
| DOMSEC-C08 | 05_domsec | decision | consensus | Prefer Element.setHTML (Sanitizer API) over innerHTML when injecting untrusted HTML, and keep a fallback while availability is limited. | - |
| DOMSEC-C09 | 05_domsec | practice | consensus | Treat setHTMLUnsafe and the other Unsafe-suffixed methods as injection sinks: they sanitize nothing by default and are less safe than innerHTML; pass TrustedHTML. | - |
| DOMSEC-C10 | 05_domsec | js-principle | single-source | innerHTML does not execute inserted script elements, yet it stays an XSS sink; do not treat it as safe. | folklore: innerHTML is safe because script tags inserted that way do not run |
| DOMSEC-C11 | 05_domsec | decision | single-source | When untrusted HTML must be rendered, sanitize it with a reputable library instead of hand-written code; OWASP names DOMPurify. | positions: OWASP and MDN recommend DOMPurify |
| DOMSEC-C12 | 05_domsec | practice | consensus | Never modify sanitized HTML afterwards; sanitize last, immediately before insertion. | - |
| DOMSEC-C13 | 05_domsec | js-principle | consensus | A sanitizer's verdict on a string is valid only for the parse it simulated: mutation XSS exploits the round trip through innerHTML, so test output in the target parser, never by string filtering alone. | folklore: a string that passes an HTML filter is safe wherever it is later rendered |
| DOMSEC-C14 | 05_domsec | practice | single-source | Treat the HTML sanitizer as a security-critical dependency and keep it current: its own advisory list shows repeated bypasses, and its runtime (older jsdom) can break it. | - |
| DOMSEC-C15 | 05_domsec | decision | consensus | Enforce Trusted Types (require-trusted-types-for 'script') so injection sinks reject plain strings; write code that passes Trusted values. | boundary: web-architecture (the CSP header deployment) |
| DOMSEC-C16 | 05_domsec | js-principle | consensus | Do not mistake Trusted Types for sanitization: the API supplies no sanitizer; protection is exactly as good as the policy function you write. | folklore: Trusted Types sanitizes input by itself |
| DOMSEC-C17 | 05_domsec | decision | contested | Use named Trusted Types policies; reserve the default policy for migration of legacy code and for third-party code that cannot be changed. | positions: MDN and web.dev: default policy only transitional or last resort; Roth et al. (USENIX 2024): with third-party code only a default policy works in practice |
| DOMSEC-C18 | 05_domsec | practice | single-source | Roll Trusted Types out in report-only mode, fix violations by refactoring, then enforce. | - |
| DOMSEC-C19 | 05_domsec | practice | single-source | Avoid TrustedScript sinks by design and never reuse an HTML sanitizer for script or URL sinks: script sanitization is hard to impossible. | - |
| DOMSEC-C20 | 05_domsec | practice | single-source | Trusted Types is Baseline newly available since February 2026; for older browsers a tinyfill gives the same protection if the code was tested with enforcement in a supporting browser. | - |
| DOMSEC-C21 | 05_domsec | decision | single-source | Mozilla's standards position on Trusted Types has been positive since 2023-12-13, with stated concerns about getPropertyType, getAttributeType and the non-standard beforepolicycreation event. | positions: Mozilla positive with concerns |
| DOMSEC-C22 | 05_domsec | decision | single-source | Google reported deploying Trusted Types on 130 services with no client-side XSS in the protected applications. | - |
| DOMSEC-C23 | 05_domsec | practice | consensus | A Trusted Types createHTML callback may wrap a vetted sanitizer, and DOMPurify can return TrustedHTML directly via RETURN_TRUSTED_TYPE. | - |
| DOMSEC-C24 | 05_domsec | practice | consensus | Treat script-URL sinks (script.src, Worker and SharedWorker constructors, importScripts, serviceWorker.register) as injection sinks and pass only allowlisted or Trusted URLs. | - |
| DOMSEC-C25 | 05_domsec | practice | contested | Do not treat setAttribute as unconditionally safe: set event-handler attributes never from untrusted data. | positions: OWASP DOM XSS sheet: setAttribute is a safe construction method; MDN Trusted Types API: setAttribute value is a TrustedScript sink, condition: attribute is an event handler (inferred) |
| DOMSEC-C26 | 05_domsec | principle | consensus | Treat CSP as a second layer behind secure code, not a first line of defense against injection. | boundary: web-architecture |
| DOMSEC-C27 | 05_domsec | practice | consensus | Write code that survives a strict CSP: no inline script, no inline event-handler attributes (use addEventListener), no string eval. | boundary: web-architecture (policy deployment) |
| DOMSEC-C28 | 05_domsec | decision | consensus | Prefer nonce or hash based strict CSP over domain allowlists: allowlists were bypassable in most deployed policies. | boundary: web-architecture; folklore: a CSP with a domain allowlist stops XSS |
| DOMSEC-C29 | 05_domsec | practice | single-source | Generate nonces in a real HTML templating engine, never in middleware that stamps every script tag. | boundary: web-architecture |
| DOMSEC-C30 | 05_domsec | practice | single-source | Register a message event listener only if you expect cross-origin messages. | - |
| DOMSEC-C31 | 05_domsec | practice | consensus | In message handlers verify event.origin (and source where relevant) before acting, and discard messages from untrusted origins. | - |
| DOMSEC-C32 | 05_domsec | practice | consensus | Compare the origin by exact match against an allowlist of full origins; substring or indexOf tests are insecure. | - |
| DOMSEC-C33 | 05_domsec | practice | consensus | After verifying the origin, validate the syntax and type of every message; a trusted sender can itself be compromised. | - |
| DOMSEC-C34 | 05_domsec | practice | consensus | Pass an exact targetOrigin to postMessage, never '*', whenever the message carries anything confidential. | - |
| DOMSEC-C35 | 05_domsec | practice | consensus | Never keep authentication tokens, session identifiers or other credentials in localStorage or sessionStorage. | boundary: web-architecture (session and token architecture) |
| DOMSEC-C36 | 05_domsec | js-principle | consensus | Treat Web Storage as readable by every script of the origin: any XSS can read all of it, so it holds no secrets. | - |
| DOMSEC-C37 | 05_domsec | practice | single-source | Validate data read from web storage and from messages as untrusted input, since attackers can write into them. | - |
| DOMSEC-C38 | 05_domsec | practice | consensus | Pin externally hosted scripts and styles to static, versioned files and protect them with Subresource Integrity. | - |
| DOMSEC-C39 | 05_domsec | practice | consensus | Write SRI as integrity="sha384-..." (sha256, sha384, sha512 allowed; avoid MD5 and SHA-1) plus crossorigin, and serve the page over a secure context. | - |
| DOMSEC-C40 | 05_domsec | practice | consensus | Expect SRI to break on vendor updates and to fail without CORS on the vendor host; it protects only content you reviewed, so pin versions. | - |
| DOMSEC-C41 | 05_domsec | principle | consensus | Treat every third-party script as code you run with your page's authority: it is rarely reviewed, and compromise of its host injects arbitrary content. | - |
| DOMSEC-C42 | 05_domsec | practice | single-source | Do not rely on a data layer as a sandbox for tag managers: container tags can still run custom JavaScript and HTML and deploy instantly. | - |
| DOMSEC-C43 | 05_domsec | decision | consensus | Isolate vendor scripts in an iframe from a different origin so they cannot reach the host DOM or cookies. | - |
| DOMSEC-C44 | 05_domsec | practice | consensus | Embed untrusted content in an iframe with the sandbox attribute and lift only the restrictions you need. | - |
| DOMSEC-C45 | 05_domsec | practice | single-source | Never combine allow-scripts and allow-same-origin on a same-origin embedded document: it can remove its own sandbox. | - |
| DOMSEC-C46 | 05_domsec | practice | single-source | Serve untrusted content from a separate origin as well, because a sandbox is useless if the content is opened outside the frame. | - |
| DOMSEC-C47 | 05_domsec | practice | contested | Links with target=_blank get noopener behaviour by default under the HTML Standard unless rel=opener is present; explicit rel=noopener noreferrer remains OWASP's advice. | folklore: every target=_blank link needs rel=noopener added; positions: HTML Standard: implied unless rel=opener; OWASP HTML5 sheet: add rel=noopener explicitly, condition: browsers that predate the implied behaviour (inferred) |
| DOMSEC-C48 | 05_domsec | js-principle | consensus | DOM clobbering is HTML-only injection: elements with an id or name overwrite globals or window and document properties, so sanitizing scripts and handlers is not enough. | folklore: XSS needs script elements or event handlers |
| DOMSEC-C49 | 05_domsec | practice | consensus | Check the type of document and window properties before sensitive use (instanceof) and declare variables explicitly. | - |
| DOMSEC-C50 | 05_domsec | practice | consensus | Do not store application globals on window or document; use local const and let variables and object properties. | - |
| DOMSEC-C51 | 05_domsec | practice | single-source | When sanitizing, neutralize id and name attributes (DOMPurify SANITIZE_NAMED_PROPS, or Sanitizer removeAttribute). | - |
| DOMSEC-C52 | 05_domsec | practice | single-source | Use Object.freeze on application-owned configuration, knowing it is shallow and no substitute for sanitization or local variables. | - |
| DOMSEC-C53 | 05_domsec | principle | single-source | DOM clobbering is common in the wild: 9,467 vulnerable data flows on 491 of the Tranco top 5K sites (2023 study). | - |
| DOMSEC-C54 | 05_domsec | principle | single-source | DOM XSS is common in the wild: 6,167 unique flaws over 480 domains, 9.6 percent of the Alexa top 5000 (2013 study). | - |
| DOMSEC-C55 | 05_domsec | practice | consensus | Rely on framework default output encoding, and treat escape hatches (dangerouslySetInnerHTML, bypassSecurityTrust*, unsafeHTML) as sinks that need sanitized input. | - |
| DOMSEC-C56 | 05_domsec | practice | single-source | Redirect automatically only to destinations on an allowlist. | - |
| DOMSEC-C57 | 05_domsec | practice | single-source | Validate URLs by parsing with the URL parser and allowlisting scheme and origin, not by substring tests. | - |
| DOMSEC-C58 | 05_domsec | practice | single-source | Register service workers only from your own origin, serve the script over HTTPS, and keep sensitive responses out of the Cache API. | - |
| DOMSEC-C59 | 05_domsec | practice | single-source | Do not use JSONP and keep authorization-dependent data out of script resources. | boundary: web-architecture |
| DOMSEC-C60 | 05_domsec | practice | consensus | Allow specific origins in Access-Control-Allow-Origin, never the wildcard on authenticated resources. | boundary: web-architecture |
| RUNSEC-C01 | 06_runsec | principle | consensus | Treat prototype pollution as the application's responsibility: validate and sanitize attacker-influenced input yourself, because Node.js core does not classify pollution that needs attacker-controlled input as a core vulnerability. | folklore: Node core will fix prototype pollution for you |
| RUNSEC-C02 | 06_runsec | js-principle | consensus | Never perform dynamic nested property writes of the form obj[key1][key2] = value with untrusted keys; if unavoidable, reject the keys __proto__, constructor and prototype before writing. | - |
| RUNSEC-C03 | 06_runsec | practice | consensus | Never pass untrusted input to a recursive merge, deep clone or set-by-path helper that does not filter prototype-reaching keys. | - |
| RUNSEC-C04 | 06_runsec | practice | consensus | Prefer Map or Set over plain objects for dictionaries keyed by untrusted strings. | - |
| RUNSEC-C05 | 06_runsec | practice | consensus | When a plain object must hold untrusted keys, create it without a prototype with Object.create(null); the literal form { __proto__: null } is the weaker alternative. | positions: OWASP Prototype Pollution sheet: literal { __proto__: null } only as last resort; MDN: both forms listed as one defence |
| RUNSEC-C06 | 06_runsec | practice | consensus | Validate untrusted structured input against a schema that rejects unneeded properties (additionalProperties false) before it reaches merge or lookup code. | boundary: 02 TYPES |
| RUNSEC-C07 | 06_runsec | practice | consensus | Read untrusted-keyed properties with Object.hasOwn and iterate with Object.keys or for...of, not for...in, so inherited (possibly polluted) properties are not visited. | - |
| RUNSEC-C08 | 06_runsec | practice | consensus | Do not rely on --disable-proto as the only pollution defence: it removes the __proto__ entry point but constructor.prototype stays reachable. | folklore: --disable-proto fixes prototype pollution |
| RUNSEC-C09 | 06_runsec | decision | consensus | Freeze built-in prototypes or lock down the realm only where the environment is high-sensitivity and tested for breakage, and remember Object.freeze is shallow. | folklore: Object.freeze makes nested data immutable |
| RUNSEC-C10 | 06_runsec | principle | consensus | Treat a pollution bug as potentially remote code execution on Node, not only as a logic error, because universal gadgets in Node core APIs turn pollution into code execution. | - |
| RUNSEC-C11 | 06_runsec | practice | single-source | Assume third-party npm packages contain pollution flaws and keep them patched, because static analysis found many previously unknown ones. | boundary: 07 SUPPLY |
| RUNSEC-C12 | 06_runsec | practice | single-source | Avoid the __proto__ accessor in new code; use Object.getPrototypeOf and Object.setPrototypeOf. | - |
| RUNSEC-C13 | 06_runsec | js-principle | consensus | Do not assume JSON.parse output is safe to merge: a parsed "__proto__" key becomes an ordinary own property and pollutes when the object is later merged or assigned into another object. | folklore: JSON.parse of untrusted JSON is inherently safe |
| RUNSEC-C14 | 06_runsec | principle | consensus | Never build code from strings: eval, new Function and string arguments to setTimeout or setInterval execute attacker-influenced input as code with the caller's privileges. | - |
| RUNSEC-C15 | 06_runsec | practice | consensus | Parse data with JSON.parse, never eval; replace eval with bracket property access, callbacks or functions instead of string code. | - |
| RUNSEC-C16 | 06_runsec | js-principle | consensus | Do not treat new Function as a safe replacement for eval: it is also an injection sink and only differs in running in global scope. | folklore: new Function is a safe alternative to eval |
| RUNSEC-C17 | 06_runsec | practice | single-source | If dynamic evaluation is unavoidable, prefer indirect eval with a "use strict" prefix over direct eval, because direct eval reads and mutates the surrounding scope and blocks engine optimizations. | - |
| RUNSEC-C18 | 06_runsec | practice | single-source | Enforce the no-code-from-strings rule statically with the no-eval, no-implied-eval and no-new-func lint rules. | boundary: 08 QUALITY |
| RUNSEC-C19 | 06_runsec | practice | consensus | In browsers, pass TrustedScript objects instead of strings to eval and Function, and prefer the trusted-types-eval CSP keyword over unsafe-eval. | boundary: 05 DOMSEC |
| RUNSEC-C20 | 06_runsec | practice | single-source | Do not rely on --disallow-code-generation-from-strings to cover node:vm: the flag makes eval and new Function throw but does not affect the vm module. | - |
| RUNSEC-C21 | 06_runsec | practice | single-source | Expect injection APIs to be common in dependencies: in a 2018 study of 235,850 npm modules, eval was used by 9,111 and exec by 7,686. | boundary: 07 SUPPLY |
| RUNSEC-C22 | 06_runsec | js-principle | single-source | Never use node:vm to run untrusted code: it is not a security mechanism. | folklore: node:vm is a sandbox for untrusted code |
| RUNSEC-C23 | 06_runsec | js-principle | consensus | Never pass unsanitized user input to child_process.exec or execSync, and do not enable the shell option of spawn, execFile and their sync forms with user input: shell metacharacters give arbitrary command execution. | - |
| RUNSEC-C24 | 06_runsec | practice | consensus | Prefer spawn or execFile with an argument array over exec when running a single program, so arguments are never parsed by a shell. | - |
| RUNSEC-C25 | 06_runsec | principle | single-source | Prefer built-in library functions over invoking OS commands at all; they cannot be manipulated into other tasks. | - |
| RUNSEC-C26 | 06_runsec | principle | single-source | When an OS command is unavoidable, allowlist the executable and the arguments, and run the process with the least privilege required. | - |
| RUNSEC-C27 | 06_runsec | js-principle | single-source | Do not use path.isAbsolute, and do not treat path.normalize or path.join alone, as protection against path traversal. | folklore: path.normalize or isAbsolute sanitizes user paths |
| RUNSEC-C28 | 06_runsec | principle | consensus | Build file paths from internally generated or trusted names, not user-submitted filenames; if user filenames must be used, apply strict allowlist validation and sanitization. | - |
| RUNSEC-C29 | 06_runsec | practice | single-source | Canonicalize a path (resolve it, following symlinks) before checking that it lies under the intended base directory; a lexical prefix check on an unresolved path is insufficient. | - |
| RUNSEC-C30 | 06_runsec | practice | consensus | Bound the length of untrusted input before regex matching, and bound repetition counts in the pattern. | - |
| RUNSEC-C31 | 06_runsec | js-principle | consensus | Write patterns without nested quantifiers or ambiguous alternation over the same characters, because crafted non-matching input forces exponential backtracking. | - |
| RUNSEC-C32 | 06_runsec | js-principle | single-source | Do not treat anti-pattern checks as proof either way: nested-quantifier heuristics rarely miss a vulnerable regex but flag many safe ones. | folklore: a regex with a nested quantifier is necessarily vulnerable |
| RUNSEC-C33 | 06_runsec | decision | consensus | Prefer a non-backtracking regex engine where one is available, and do not assume V8 offers one: V8's is experimental, behind flags and unsupported for backreferences, lookarounds and the u and i flags (status as of 2021). | - |
| RUNSEC-C34 | 06_runsec | practice | single-source | Treat a regex match timeout as a validation failure, not as a pass. | - |
| RUNSEC-C35 | 06_runsec | js-principle | single-source | Require the regex to match the entire value when validating; JavaScript ^ and $ are anchors where $ is not permissive about a trailing newline. | - |
| RUNSEC-C36 | 06_runsec | js-principle | consensus | Treat regex matching on untrusted input as an availability risk for Node servers, since one request can block the single-threaded event loop for seconds. | boundary: 03 ASYNC |
| RUNSEC-C37 | 06_runsec | practice | single-source | Keep Node.js on a release containing the CVE-2026-21717 fix and treat parsing large untrusted JSON as a denial-of-service surface. | - |
| RUNSEC-C38 | 06_runsec | decision | contested | Do not treat the permission model as a sandbox against malicious code; use it as a seat belt for trusted code. | positions: SRC-128 permissions API: seat belt for trusted code, no guarantees against malicious code; SRC-140 threat model: not a boundary against intentional misuse or a compromised process; SRC-078 best practices: can help contain the impact of malicious or compromised dependencies. Condition: defence in depth for trusted code versus containment of hostile code. Stability labels also differ: permissions page says stable since v23.5.0 and v22.13.0, CLI page labels --permission and --allow-child-process Stability 1.1 Active development |
| RUNSEC-C39 | 06_runsec | practice | consensus | When using --permission, ensure no granted path contains a relative symlink, and do not rely on it to restrict code that already holds open file descriptors. | - |
| RUNSEC-C40 | 06_runsec | practice | single-source | Grant the permission model the narrowest paths and capabilities needed and avoid the allow-all wildcard (*). | - |
| RUNSEC-C41 | 06_runsec | principle | consensus | Assume every module in a Node process is fully trusted by the runtime: any code in the process can run arbitrary code with eval, and write access to the file system achieves the same, so there is no in-process privilege boundary against dependencies. | boundary: 07 SUPPLY |
| RUNSEC-C42 | 06_runsec | principle | consensus | Validate every external input in application code before it reaches Node or language APIs, using an allowlist of what is accepted. | boundary: 02 TYPES |
| RUNSEC-C43 | 06_runsec | principle | consensus | Prefer a pure data format such as JSON over formats that can carry types or code when exchanging data across a trust boundary, and never deserialize untrusted data into executable structures. | - |
| RUNSEC-C44 | 06_runsec | principle | single-source | Sign serialized messages when the set of expected messages is known, and verify before deserializing. | - |
| RUNSEC-C45 | 06_runsec | practice | single-source | Document where dangerous functionality (untrusted deserialization, dynamic code execution, raw binary parsing) is used in the application. | - |
| RUNSEC-C46 | 06_runsec | principle | consensus | Never hardcode secrets in source code or committed configuration files. | - |
| RUNSEC-C47 | 06_runsec | decision | majority | Treat environment variables as a weaker channel for secrets than a dedicated secrets mechanism, and remember that every module in the process can read them. | folklore: environment variables are a safe place for secrets |
| RUNSEC-C48 | 06_runsec | practice | single-source | Run secret detection before commit and rotate secrets regularly. | boundary: 08 QUALITY |
| SUPPLY-C01 | 07_supply | principle | consensus | Treat every dependency, direct or transitive, as trusted code running with the application's full privileges, and treat malicious or compromised dependencies as a first-order application risk. | - |
| SUPPLY-C02 | 07_supply | js-principle | majority | Do not expect the Node.js runtime to contain a dependency: the permission boundary is the application's, and per-package least privilege is a research proposal, not a shipped default. | boundary: RUNSEC |
| SUPPLY-C03 | 07_supply | practice | consensus | Commit the lockfile to version control so every install, in CI and deployment included, resolves the same tree. | - |
| SUPPLY-C04 | 07_supply | practice | consensus | Install in CI and production with `npm ci` (or the package manager's frozen-lockfile equivalent), never `npm install`, so a lockfile and manifest mismatch fails instead of being silently resolved. | - |
| SUPPLY-C05 | 07_supply | js-principle | majority | Do not rely on exact pins in package.json alone: pinning a dependency does not pin its transitive dependencies, which only the lockfile fixes. | - |
| SUPPLY-C06 | 07_supply | decision | contested | CONTESTED: whether to pin dependencies exactly, allow ranges, or rely on the lockfile; admitted sources disagree and the conditions differ. | positions: Node.js security guide: pin to a specific immutable version, not a range; OWASP SSC cheat sheet: limit to a verified version via lockfile; OpenSSF npm guide v1.1: allow minimum-to-latest range such as caret or tilde; He et al. 2025: direct pinning can increase malicious-update exposure in larger graphs, prefer collective ecosystem pinning; condition: size of dependency graph, library versus application |
| SUPPLY-C07 | 07_supply | practice | single-source | Review lockfile diffs as part of code review, because lockfile poisoning is a listed attack vector and the lockfile carries resolved URLs and integrity hashes. | - |
| SUPPLY-C08 | 07_supply | practice | single-source | Under npm 12 and later, dependency install scripts are blocked by default; approve only reviewed packages, pinned to the exact version, through the allowScripts policy. | - |
| SUPPLY-C09 | 07_supply | practice | consensus | On npm before v12, and wherever scripts still run by default, disable lifecycle scripts for installs with `--ignore-scripts` or `ignore-scripts=true`, and allowlist the few packages that need them. | boundary: tool-version scope, advice applies to npm before v12 only |
| SUPPLY-C10 | 07_supply | decision | consensus | Expect dependency build scripts to be blocked by default in current package managers (npm 12, pnpm 10 and later), and maintain an explicit allowlist rather than disabling the guard globally. | - |
| SUPPLY-C11 | 07_supply | practice | single-source | Under npm 12, git-referenced and tarball-URL dependencies are refused unless allowed; set allow-git or allow-remote to root rather than all when a project needs them. | - |
| SUPPLY-C12 | 07_supply | decision | consensus | Where a release-age cooldown exists (npm min-release-age from v11.10.0, pnpm minimumReleaseAge default 1440 minutes, Dependabot cooldown default 3 days), consider enabling it so freshly published versions are not installed at once. | - |
| SUPPLY-C13 | 07_supply | decision | single-source | The effectiveness of a release-age cooldown rests on one T1 assertion and vendor figures; no peer-reviewed measurement of time-to-removal was found. | - |
| SUPPLY-C14 | 07_supply | practice | single-source | Keep security updates outside any cooldown: Dependabot's cooldown applies to version updates only and its default does not apply to security updates. | - |
| SUPPLY-C15 | 07_supply | decision | consensus | When publishing an npm package from CI, prefer trusted publishing (OIDC, short-lived workflow-specific credentials) over long-lived tokens. | - |
| SUPPLY-C16 | 07_supply | decision | single-source | On npm, publishing tokens are narrowing: legacy tokens are removed (Nov 2025), bypass-2FA tokens lose account-governance rights (Aug 2026), direct publishing with a granular token ends (Jan 2027); plan publishing around trusted publishing or stage-only tokens. | - |
| SUPPLY-C17 | 07_supply | practice | consensus | Enable two-factor authentication on registry publishing accounts; phishing-resistant MFA on developer accounts is the response CISA recommends after account compromises. | - |
| SUPPLY-C18 | 07_supply | js-principle | single-source | Never read npm provenance as a safety verdict: provenance links a package to its source and build, it does not guarantee absence of malicious code. | folklore: a package with provenance is safe |
| SUPPLY-C19 | 07_supply | js-principle | single-source | Do not treat registry signatures as protection against a malicious publisher: they detect tampering of tarball content by a registry mirror or proxy, verified with `npm audit signatures`. | folklore: a signed package is a trustworthy package |
| SUPPLY-C20 | 07_supply | practice | single-source | To get npm provenance, publish from a cloud-hosted GitHub Actions runner with `id-token: write` and `--provenance`; under trusted publishing it is generated automatically for public repositories and packages. | - |
| SUPPLY-C21 | 07_supply | practice | single-source | Run `npm audit` against the committed lockfile and set `audit-level` to define the failing severity; without a lockfile results can differ on every run. | - |
| SUPPLY-C22 | 07_supply | js-principle | consensus | Treat audit findings as triage input, not as a measure of exploitability: most package-level findings are unreachable and most alerts concern dependencies not shipped to production. | folklore: every npm audit finding is an exploitable risk |
| SUPPLY-C23 | 07_supply | js-principle | single-source | Do not use the dependencies versus devDependencies split to judge what ships to production: 59 percent of runtime-configured dependencies were not used in production and 28.2 percent of dev-configured ones were. | folklore: devDependencies never reach production |
| SUPPLY-C24 | 07_supply | practice | consensus | Check dependency names for typos and for a more popular look-alike before adding a package, and verify the package exists and is authentic. | - |
| SUPPLY-C25 | 07_supply | js-principle | single-source | Do not reduce package confusion to typing mistakes: a study of 1,200+ attacks found 13 confusion mechanisms, many semantic rather than syntactic. | folklore: typosquatting is just typing mistakes |
| SUPPLY-C26 | 07_supply | practice | single-source | Publish internal packages under an owned scope and route that scope to the private registry in .npmrc, so a public package cannot shadow an internal name. | - |
| SUPPLY-C27 | 07_supply | practice | single-source | Before adding a dependency, ask whether existing components suffice, and test it in isolation for unexpected indirect dependencies in production. | - |
| SUPPLY-C28 | 07_supply | practice | majority | Judge maintenance before adopting a package: recent activity and release within 12 months, more than one maintainer, and awareness that a few accounts or inactive maintainers are a measured weak link. | - |
| SUPPLY-C29 | 07_supply | practice | majority | Treat install scripts as a risk signal when evaluating a package. | - |
| SUPPLY-C30 | 07_supply | js-principle | single-source | Plan for expired maintainer email domains as a takeover route: a study found 2,818 maintainer addresses on expired domains, making 8,494 packages potentially hijackable. | - |
| SUPPLY-C31 | 07_supply | principle | consensus | Assume the recurring route is takeover of maintainer accounts or maintainership, not a vulnerable library: incidents include the 2018 event-stream handover, the 2018 eslint-scope token theft, the 2025 debug phishing and the 2025 Shai-Hulud worm. | - |
| SUPPLY-C32 | 07_supply | principle | single-source | Layer controls rather than rely on one: attack trees list 107 vectors across code contribution to distribution, mapped to 33 safeguards. | - |
| SUPPLY-C33 | 07_supply | decision | single-source | Read supply-chain levels as graded: SLSA Build L1 provenance exists, L2 hosted platform signs it, L3 hardened builds resist tampering during the build. | - |
| SUPPLY-C34 | 07_supply | decision | single-source | Keyless signing with ephemeral keys tied to an OIDC identity and a transparency log lowers the key-management burden of artifact signing. | - |
| SUPPLY-C35 | 07_supply | decision | single-source | Use OpenSSF Scorecard results only as per-check evidence: it rates Pinned-Dependencies at Medium risk and Dependency-Update-Tool, Signed-Releases, Token-Permissions, Binary-Artifacts at High, several checks run only on GitHub repositories, and a score never proves a package safe. | - |
| SUPPLY-C36 | 07_supply | practice | majority | Run an automated dependency-update and vulnerability-alert mechanism, with security updates enabled and kept separate from feature updates, because bundled fixes hinder adoption. | - |
| SUPPLY-C37 | 07_supply | practice | single-source | Generate and consume SBOMs automatically in CI, and accept only signed components whose signatures are validated before use. | - |
| SUPPLY-C38 | 07_supply | practice | consensus | Give CI tokens least privilege and keep secrets out of repositories and out of published tarballs; check tarball contents with `npm publish --dry-run`. | boundary: RUNSEC |
| SUPPLY-C39 | 07_supply | practice | single-source | Do not copy README examples into production without a security review. | - |
| SUPPLY-C40 | 07_supply | js-principle | single-source | Do not assume lockfile semantics are the same across package managers: a study of 7 managers found a wide variety of generation and content decisions, and developers struggle to maintain them. | - |
| SUPPLY-C41 | 07_supply | practice | single-source | After a worm-style compromise, CISA's position is to review lockfiles, rotate all developer credentials and pin to versions published before the incident date. | positions: CISA: pin to pre-incident versions, rotate credentials, enforce phishing-resistant MFA |
| SUPPLY-C42 | 07_supply | decision | single-source | A trust-downgrade check can block a version whose publishing trust level dropped relative to earlier releases (pnpm trustPolicy no-downgrade). | - |
| QUALITY-C01 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Configure ESLint with a flat-config file named eslint.config.js (or .mjs or .cjs) at the project root exporting an array of configuration objects. | - |
| QUALITY-C02 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Scope rules with files and ignores in config objects; where several objects match a file they merge with later objects winning, so order configs from general to specific. | - |
| QUALITY-C03 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Start from ESLint's recommended config (from @eslint/js) as the baseline rule set, since the rules index marks which rules it enables. | - |
| QUALITY-C04 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Use typescript-eslint's recommended config as the drop-in baseline for TypeScript code, with stylistic as a separate opt-in set that does not affect program logic. | - |
| QUALITY-C05 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Make CI fail on lint warnings, not only errors, by passing --max-warnings 0; without it warnings never change the exit status. | - |
| QUALITY-C06 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Treat ESLint exit code 2 as a broken tool or configuration, distinct from exit code 1 (lint findings), when scripting CI. | - |
| QUALITY-C07 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Report unused eslint-disable directives (--report-unused-disable-directives, or the -severity variant, default warn) so obsolete suppressions cannot hide future errors. | - |
| QUALITY-C08 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Use ESLint's --cache for repeated runs; choose --cache-strategy content when file modification times change without content changes (for example fresh CI checkouts). | - |
| QUALITY-C09 | 08_quality | decision | single-source | Extend typescript-eslint's strict config only if a nontrivial share of the developers are highly proficient in TypeScript, and expect its rule set to change outside major versions because it is not semver-stable. | positions: typescript-eslint: strict only for proficient teams |
| QUALITY-C10 | 08_quality | decision | single-source | Enable typed linting (parserOptions.projectService) to get rules that need type information, such as no-floating-promises, and budget for its cost: TypeScript must analyze the whole project before linting. | boundary: 03_async (rule no-floating-promises) |
| QUALITY-C11 | 08_quality | decision | consensus | Do not rely on ESLint core for formatting: its formatting rules are deprecated and replaced by @stylistic equivalents, because the core team could not sustain them. | - |
| QUALITY-C12 | 08_quality | decision | single-source | Use a dedicated source formatter for layout rather than a linter, because a formatter understands the whole file and applies consistent formatting throughout; the ESLint TSC names Prettier, dprint, or the @stylistic plugin as the options. | positions: ESLint TSC: dedicated formatter or @stylistic |
| QUALITY-C13 | 08_quality | decision | contested | Formatter choice is open: ESLint's TSC recommends Prettier, dprint or @stylistic, while Biome documents one tool whose formatter handles all formatting decisions beside its linter; no admitted source ranks them. | positions: ESLint TSC: Prettier, dprint or @stylistic; Biome docs: one tool for lint and format; Prettier docs: run Prettier separately from linters |
| QUALITY-C14 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Prettier only prints code and never transforms it, so import sorting, brace insertion and similar changes belong to lint rules, not the formatter; printWidth is a guideline, not a hard limit. | - |
| QUALITY-C15 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | When pairing Prettier with ESLint, disable conflicting rules with eslint-config-prettier and run Prettier separately; Prettier states eslint-plugin-prettier is generally not recommended (red squiggles, slower, extra layer). | positions: Prettier: run it directly and use eslint-config-prettier only |
| QUALITY-C16 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Check formatting in CI with prettier --check (exit 0 formatted, 1 not formatted, 2 tool failure) and add a pre-commit hook to cut CI failures from formatting. | - |
| QUALITY-C17 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Review Biome's unsafe fixes by hand before applying them: only safe fixes are guaranteed not to change semantics, and type-aware rules switch on Biome's scanner only when enabled. | - |
| QUALITY-C18 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Do not suppress type or lint errors with @ts-ignore, @ts-expect-error or @ts-nocheck; where a lint suppression is legitimate (for example any in a test mock), add a comment documenting why. | positions: Google TS guide: no suppression directives |
| QUALITY-C19 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Google's JavaScript guide requires braces on all control structures and a semicolon on every statement, forbidding reliance on automatic semicolon insertion. | positions: Google JS guide: semicolons required |
| QUALITY-C20 | 08_quality | principle | single-source | Enable a linter or safe language mode and address its warnings; the OpenSSF passing criteria make this a MUST. | - |
| QUALITY-C21 | 08_quality | principle | single-source | Apply at least one static-analysis tool beyond compiler warnings to every proposed major production release. | - |
| QUALITY-C22 | 08_quality | principle | single-source | Keep a policy that new major functionality gets automated tests, and keep evidence that recent major changes followed it; make the suite invocable in the language's standard way. | - |
| QUALITY-C23 | 08_quality | principle | single-source | Combine several analysis tools in CI, but not as the only mechanism, and write negative tests (what should not happen does not) so that passing the suite means shipping. | positions: OpenSSF Best Practices WG |
| QUALITY-C24 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | node:test ships in Node, sets exit code 1 when any test fails, and is stable from v20.0.0; its coverage flag (--experimental-test-coverage) is experimental (Stability 1), so do not gate on it as a stable feature. | - |
| QUALITY-C25 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Import assert in strict mode (node:assert/strict): legacy mode compares with == in equal and deepEqual and can pass unequal values. | folklore: assert.deepEqual is a safe equality check |
| QUALITY-C26 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Vitest facts for selection input: requires Vite 6.4 or later and Node 22.12 or later, finds files with .test. or .spec. in the name, runs in watch mode by default so use vitest run in CI. | - |
| QUALITY-C27 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Vitest offers a V8 provider (no pre-transpile step) and an Istanbul provider (instrumentation, any JavaScript runtime); since v3.2.0 V8 coverage uses AST-based remapping. | - |
| QUALITY-C28 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Jest needs a transform (Babel presets or ts-jest) to run TypeScript, and finds tests by .test.js naming in its examples; these are facts about Jest only. | - |
| QUALITY-C29 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Test behaviours through the public API, one test per behaviour rather than per method, and keep tests DAMP (descriptive and meaningful phrases) over DRY. | positions: Google: public API, behaviours, DAMP |
| QUALITY-C30 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Prefer real objects over mocks when they are fast and deterministic, because brittle tests fail on unrelated changes that introduce no bug. | positions: Google: real over mocks |
| QUALITY-C31 | 08_quality | decision | single-source | Google's recommended test mix is about 80% narrow unit tests, 15% medium integration tests, 5% end-to-end; it is Google's position, not a general rule. | positions: Google: 80/15/5 |
| QUALITY-C32 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Track the flaky-test rate: Google reports about 0.15% and says tests begin to lose value near 1% flakiness. | positions: Google: 1% flakiness erodes value |
| QUALITY-C33 | 08_quality | principle | single-source | Expect flaky tests to come mostly from async waits, concurrency and test-order dependency, and to be flaky from the first run, so check new tests extensively when they are added. | - |
| QUALITY-C34 | 08_quality | practice | majority | Wait on a condition, not a fixed delay, in asynchronous tests: the flaky-test study found 54% of Async Wait flakes fixed with waitFor, and Playwright's locators and web-first assertions retry until the condition holds. | - |
| QUALITY-C35 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Clean the shared state between tests, because 74% of order-dependent flaky tests in the study were fixed that way. | - |
| QUALITY-C36 | 08_quality | decision | contested | Do not use a coverage percentage as a quality target; use coverage to find under-tested code, because its correlation with suite effectiveness is low to moderate once suite size is controlled. | positions: Inozemtseva and Holmes: no coverage target, use it to find untested code; OpenSSF passing criteria: SUGGESTED that suites cover most or all branches and inputs; folklore: high coverage means effective tests |
| QUALITY-C37 | 08_quality | principle | consensus | Read a mutation score as the share of injected faults that tests kill: mutation analysis measures whether tests detect small seeded changes, which coverage cannot show. | - |
| QUALITY-C38 | 08_quality | decision | single-source | When adopting mutation testing at scale, run it incrementally on changed code during code review and filter mutants, instead of mutating the whole code base. | positions: Google: incremental mutation at review |
| QUALITY-C39 | 08_quality | principle | consensus | Property-based testing replaces hand-picked inputs with generated ones: a property is a checkable statement, inputs are generated at random, and failures are shrunk to the smallest reproducing input (shrinking is fast-check's, not in the QuickCheck paper). | - |
| QUALITY-C40 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Control the distribution of generated test data with custom generators: random testing is most effective when the distribution follows actual data, and a uniform distribution is often a poor default. | - |
| QUALITY-C41 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Properties double as checkable documentation, so write them beside the code they test. | - |
| QUALITY-C42 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Install with npm ci in CI: it requires a package-lock.json, exits with an error when lock and package.json disagree, removes node_modules first, and never writes either file. | boundary: 07_supply |
| QUALITY-C43 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Remember that GitHub required status checks pass on successful, skipped or neutral; make the gate job always run so a skipped check cannot let a merge through. | - |
| QUALITY-C44 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Scorecard rewards tests before merge (CI-Tests, low risk), SAST (medium), Fuzzing (medium), human code review (high) and branch protection (high), but each is detected only on GitHub or by listed tools, so a score is not evidence that a project is safe. | positions: Scorecard: risk levels as its own rating |
| QUALITY-C45 | 08_quality | practice | single-source | Treat eslint-plugin-security findings as hotspots needing human triage, not as verdicts: its maintainers state it finds a lot of false positives. | boundary: 06_runsec |
| QUALITY-C46 | 08_quality | decision | single-source | The OpenSSF concise guide recommends a dependency-update cooldown of about three days, saying cooldowns counter most malicious package releases; the origin of that figure is not yet found, so do not use it as evidence. | boundary: 07_supply; positions: OpenSSF Best Practices WG: about 3 days |
